newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Roche on centre-stage in merger rumours.
newsitem.headline: Roche on centre-stage in merger rumours.

text.p: Talk of Swiss group Roche as a buyer looking for a takeover is making the rounds again as speculators try to guess the next move in a global consolidation process among pharmaceutical makers.

Within the past two days Roche has been named as a possible suitor for Smithkline Beecham Plc and for Sweden's Astra AB. In the past it was repeatedly rumoured to be a potential suitor for Britain's Zeneca Group Plc.
Despite the rumours, analysts and players in the market, when queried individually, produce a list of reasons why the Swiss pharmaceuticals giant is probably not in play -- this time.
Take the Smithkline rumour for example. Speculation was also circulating that Roche was trying to put together a funding package of up to 50 billion Swiss francs.
A monumental deal of this kind could cost the company something in the neighborhood of five billion per annum in interest and amortisation alone, one industry executive said.
In addition, in the case of a company like Smithkline, goodwill writeoffs would be considerable.
"People actually believe they (Roche) have this kind of money," the executive said.

But these rumours play against the belief that, because of the vast -- and rising -- costs of new product development, in future only companies in possession of some four to five percent of global market share will be in a position to survive.
Only two companies have managed this to date -- Glaxo Wellcome and Novartis.

Following the 1995 mega-merger which formed Glaxo-Wellcome Plc and this year's planned merger of Swiss drug groups Ciba-Geigy AG and Sandoz AG, industry watchers are trying to envision the next mega-deal.
Roche has all the qualities of a company preparing for the hunt. It has some 15 billion francs in cash on its books and has said it is willing to consider a strategic purchase, if the price is right.
"The market expects and wants Roche to do something," one share broker said.
But the company's healthy new product pipeline means it is under no pressure to act quickly. In fact, analysts say it is probably positioned well enough to thrive for the next four or five years.

Roche has said on numerous occasions it wants to grow primarily from internal resources but that it is ready to explore opportunities which arise if they make sense in terms of strategic fit and if the price is right.
However, Roche derives as much as a quarter of its profits from its investment portfolio.

It is highly unlikely that it will expand to the prescribed critical mass of four to five percent market share from the current 2.6 percent from internal growth, said Bank Julius Baer analyst Beat Alpiger.
Thus follows the conclusion that the company would prefer reducing the portion of income derived from financials and look to expand either through an acquisition or joint venture.
"They don't want to be a bank," Bear's Alpiger said.
But a quick merger play is also unlikely given Roche's capital structure, Alpiger also said.

The group's share capital consists of 1.6 million 100 franc nominal value shares, of which some 50 percent are held by insiders and between 13 and 14 percent by BZ Group's Pharma Vision investment trust.

It also has just over seven million participation certificates outstanding, meaning that some 80 percent of its capitalisation is in non-voting securities. Not a very attractive structure to bring to a merger, notes Alpinger.
Nonetheless, conventional wisdom says something considerable must come from the Roche side, sooner or later.
